RTD vs Thermistor: Range, Accuracy, Sensitivity, Self Heating, Wiring and Cost Compared With a Solved Example and Slope Calculator

Both sensors change resistance with temperature, but they behave very differently once you put them in a plant or on a circuit board. This page compares them point by point so you can pick the right one with confidence.

Comparison Table IEC 60751 Classes NTC Beta Equation Self Heating Slope Calculator

An RTD and a thermistor both measure temperature through resistance, yet they differ in range, linearity, sensitivity and cost. Use the comparison table, solved example and calculator to choose the right sensor for process or electronics work.

Hello everyone, today we are going to compare rtd vs thermistor sensors and see which one suits process plants and which one suits electronics.

What Is the Difference in RTD vs Thermistor?

The RTD vs thermistor difference is that an RTD uses a pure metal, usually platinum, whose resistance rises almost linearly with temperature over a wide range of about minus 200 to 850 °C. A thermistor uses a ceramic metal oxide or polymer whose resistance changes far more sharply but non linearly, which makes it very sensitive over a narrow range, typically minus 50 to 150 °C.

PointRTD (Pt100, Pt1000)Thermistor (NTC, PTC)
MaterialPlatinum metalCeramic metal oxide
Typical rangeMinus 200 to 650 °C, up to 850 °C specialMinus 100 to 325 °C, most parts 150 °C or less
LinearityFairly linear, Callendar Van Dusen curveExponential, needs Beta or Steinhart Hart
SensitivityAbout 0.39 ohm per °C for Pt100About 4 % per °C for a 10k NTC at 25 °C
AccuracyIEC 60751 Class AA, A, B, C0.05 to 1.5 °C, best near 25 °C
Self heatingLow, 0.5 to 1 mA excitationHigher risk, keep current very low
Stability at 100 °CAbout 0.05 °C per yearAbout 0.2 °C per year
Response time1 to 50 s with sheath0.12 to 10 s, small beads are fast
Wiring2, 3 or 4 wire to cancel lead resistanceUsually 2 wire, lead error negligible
CostModerate to highLow to moderate
Typical usesProcess plants, pharma, labs, HVAC plant roomsElectronics, batteries, motors, appliances, medical

The range, accuracy, stability and response figures come from the DwyerOmega RTD vs thermistor comparison, and the 850 °C limit from a Texas Instruments application note. Treat them as typical values and confirm limits on each datasheet.

If you need a refresher on either sensor first, read how an RTD temperature sensor works and how NTC and PTC thermistors work.

How Each Sensor Converts Temperature to Resistance

An RTD is a fine platinum wire or a thin platinum film on a ceramic substrate. As the metal heats up, its lattice vibrates more and electrons scatter more, so resistance rises at a steady rate of about 0.385 % per °C for the common IEC 60751 platinum curve.

A thermistor is a semiconductor ceramic, so heat frees more charge carriers and resistance falls sharply in an NTC part. A PTC part does the opposite and can jump in resistance by orders of magnitude near its switching point, which is why it works as a protection element rather than a precision sensor.

Pt100 RTD

100 ohm at 0 °C platinum element, the standard in process plants and transmitters.

Best for: Pipes, vessels, reactors, labs
Process
Pt1000 RTD

1000 ohm at 0 °C, ten times the signal and much smaller lead wire error.

Best for: 2 wire circuits, HVAC, battery systems
Low lead error
NTC Thermistor

Resistance falls as temperature rises, high sensitivity, specified by R25 and Beta.

Best for: Electronics, chargers, medical probes
Sensitive
PTC Thermistor

Resistance jumps sharply at a switching temperature, used as a trip element.

Best for: Motor winding protection, inrush limiting
Protection
RTD (Callendar Van Dusen, t ≥ 0 °C)
R(t) = R0 (1 + A t + B t²)
A = 0.0039083
B = 0.0000005775 (subtracted)
NTC (Beta model, T in kelvin)
R(T) = R25 × e^[B (1/T minus 1/298.15)]
Slope dR/dT = R × B ÷ T² (falling)

The RTD curve above is the Callendar Van Dusen equation, where the B term is negative and below 0 °C a third C term is added. The Beta line uses absolute temperature in kelvin, and our guide on the NTC thermistor Beta equation works through step by step.

Do You Know?

DwyerOmega notes that a thermistor changes by tens of ohms per degree, while a Pt100 RTD changes by only about 0.39 ohm per degree. That large signal is why a simple voltage divider and a microcontroller ADC can read a thermistor without a precision amplifier.

Which Is More Accurate, RTD or Thermistor?

Near room temperature a good thermistor can be more accurate than a standard RTD, with interchangeable parts held to plus or minus 0.1 or 0.2 °C according to Mouser and Littelfuse. Over a wide range, however, the RTD wins, because its tolerance is defined by IEC 60751 classes and its drift stays very small.

IEC 60751 ClassTolerance FormulaAt 0 °CAt 100 °CAt 200 °C
Class AA (F 0.1)0.1 + 0.0017 |t|±0.10 °C±0.27 °C±0.44 °C
Class A (F 0.15)0.15 + 0.002 |t|±0.15 °C±0.35 °C±0.55 °C
Class B (F 0.3)0.3 + 0.005 |t|±0.30 °C±0.80 °C±1.30 °C
Class C (F 0.6)0.6 + 0.01 |t|±0.60 °C±1.60 °C±2.60 °C

Our detailed page on RTD tolerance classes in IEC 60751 explains the valid temperature range for each class, which is narrower for thin film elements. Thermistor tolerance is usually quoted as 1, 3, 5 or 10 % of R25 and widens quickly as you move away from 25 °C.

Tempco reports that precision RTDs can hold stability of 0.0025 °C per year and most industrial RTDs drift less than 0.1 °C per year. In an RTD vs thermistor decision for a custody transfer, pharma or calibration bath duty, that long term stability usually matters more than raw sensitivity.

Quick Tip

When a datasheet says a thermistor is accurate to 0.1 °C, check the temperature band. Many parts quote that figure only between 0 and 70 °C, and the error can grow several times outside it.

RTD vs Thermistor Sensitivity and Linearity

Sensitivity is the change in resistance per degree, and here the thermistor is ten times stronger in percentage terms. Linearity is how straight the resistance curve is, and here the RTD is far better, which is why the RTD vs thermistor trade off is often summed up as range and linearity against sensitivity and cost.

The calculator below compares both sensors from minus 50 to 150 °C using IEC 60751 coefficients and the Beta model.

RTD vs Thermistor Slope Calculator
Resistance and Slope
RTD 109.73 ohm, slope 0.388 ohm/°C (0.354 %/°C). NTC 10000.0 ohm, slope minus 444.4 ohm/°C (minus 4.44 %/°C)
Solved example at 25 °C
Pt100: R = 100 (1 + 0.0977 minus 0.00036)
R = 109.73 ohm
Slope = 100 (0.0039083 minus 0.0000289)
Slope = 0.388 ohm/°C = 0.354 %/°C
10k NTC, Beta 3950, T = 298.15 K
Slope = 10000 × 3950 ÷ 298.15²
Slope = 444.4 ohm/°C falling = 4.44 %/°C

So at 25 °C the 10k NTC gives roughly 12.5 times more signal per degree than the Pt100 in percentage terms. At 100 °C the NTC slope falls to about 2.8 % per °C, while the RTD slope barely changes.

If you prefer a ready made curve for a 10k part, the NTC thermistor resistance calculator on our sister site converts resistance and temperature both ways. For platinum sensors use our own RTD resistance to temperature calculator instead.

RTD vs Thermistor Self Heating and Wiring

Both sensors need an excitation current, and that current heats the element by I²R. Texas Instruments recommends keeping RTD current between 500 µA and 1 mA, and our article on RTD self heating error shows how to estimate the resulting offset from the dissipation constant.

Tempco points out that thermistors are more prone to self heating, so their measuring current must be kept low. A 10k part at 100 µA dissipates only 0.1 mW.

For a Pt100, just 1 ohm of total lead resistance in a 2 wire circuit reads as about 2.6 °C of error, which is why plants rarely use 2 wire RTDs. Compare the options in our guide to 2 wire, 3 wire and 4 wire RTD connections.

Field SymptomLikely CauseCheck or Fix
RTD reads high by a steady offset2 wire lead resistance or unequal 3 wire leadsMeasure each lead, rewire as 4 wire
NTC reads high in still airSelf heating from too much currentReduce excitation, add duty cycling
Reading jumps to full scaleOpen element or broken leadCheck resistance at the head, see burnout setting

For field checks, follow how to test an RTD Pt100 with a calibrated meter, and compare a thermistor against its R25 and Beta table instead.

RTD Strengths and Limits
  • Wide range up to 650 °C and beyond
  • Near linear, easy to linearise in a transmitter
  • Defined accuracy classes under IEC 60751
  • Very low long term drift
Thermistor Strengths and Limits
  • Very high sensitivity, simple circuits
  • Fast response with small beads
  • Low cost and small size
  • Strongly non linear, needs a lookup or equation

Is a Thermistor an RTD?

No, a thermistor is not an RTD, even though both are resistance temperature detectors in the literal sense. In industry the term RTD means a metal element following a defined curve, while thermistor means a semiconductor element with a manufacturer specific curve.

A PTC thermistor, such as the triplet sensors used for motor thermistor protection with a PTC relay, is a switching device and is not used for precise readings.

Myth: A thermistor is always more accurate than an RTD
Fact: Only near its reference temperature, over a wide span a Class A RTD is usually better
Myth: RTDs are always slow
Fact: A thin film element in a small sheath can respond in a couple of seconds
Myth: Any 4 to 20 mA transmitter accepts a thermistor
Fact: Most process transmitters accept RTD and thermocouple inputs only, check the input list

RTD vs Thermistor Applications

Process plants
Pt100 sensors in thermowells with head mounted transmitters on pipes, reactors and tanks
Electronics and power
NTC thermistors on PCBs, power modules, chargers and inverter heat sinks
Batteries and EV packs
NTC thermistors on cells, sometimes Pt1000 where wide range is needed
Motors and transformers
PTC thermistors for trip protection, Pt100 for winding temperature indication

In a plant, the RTD usually feeds a head mount temperature transmitter sending 4 to 20 mA to the DCS. On a board, a thermistor sits in a voltage divider governed by Ohm and Kirchhoff laws.

If you are still choosing between all three common sensors, read our comparisons of thermocouple vs RTD and thermistor vs thermocouple. Together with this RTD vs thermistor guide they cover nearly every resistive and voltage based contact sensor you will meet.

How to Choose: RTD vs Thermistor Selection Checklist

  • Is the process above 150 °C or below minus 50 °C, then choose an RTD
  • Do you need a defined IEC 60751 class for audits or validation, then choose an RTD
  • Do you need fast response in a tiny package on a PCB, then choose a thermistor
  • Is the cable run long with only 2 wires, then use a Pt1000 or a thermistor
  • Is the duty overtemperature trip only, then use a PTC thermistor with a relay

Also check how heat reaches the sensor through the thermowell, which our article on temperature sensor response time shows how to measure.

Quick Tip

For a Pt1000 in a 2 wire circuit, 1 ohm of lead resistance adds only about 0.26 °C of error. That simple change often removes the need for a 3 wire cable on short HVAC or battery runs.

Do You Know?

Pt100 simply means platinum with 100 ohm at 0 °C, and Pt1000 means 1000 ohm on the same curve, as our Pt100 vs Pt1000 guide shows.

Application note SNOAA67 covering RTD classes, wiring, excitation current and a linear thermistor option

The Texas Instruments note puts RTD wiring, excitation and classes next to a linear silicon thermistor, the same RTD vs thermistor question seen from the electronics side.

RTD vs Thermistor FAQ

Which is better, RTD or thermistor?

Neither sensor is better in every case, because each one suits a different duty. An RTD is better for wide range process work, while a thermistor is better for narrow range electronics where cost and sensitivity matter most.

So the RTD vs thermistor answer depends on range, accuracy class, wiring and budget. Use the checklist above and pick the sensor whose limits sit comfortably beyond your process conditions.

Which is more accurate, RTD or thermistor?

A precision thermistor can be more accurate within a small band around room temperature, sometimes to about 0.1 degree. Outside that band its error and drift grow quickly, especially at higher temperatures.

An RTD keeps a defined tolerance under IEC 60751 across a much wider span. For process, pharma and calibration work it is usually the more accurate and repeatable choice over time.

Is a thermistor faster than an RTD?

A small bead thermistor usually responds faster, with DwyerOmega quoting about 0.12 to 10 seconds. A sheathed RTD probe typically takes 1 to 50 seconds depending on its diameter and installation.

In any RTD vs thermistor speed comparison, the thermowell often dominates the response time of either sensor. A thin film RTD in a small spring loaded insert can respond almost as quickly as a sheathed thermistor.

Can I replace an RTD with a thermistor?

Only if the receiving device accepts a thermistor input and the range suits the thermistor rating. Most process transmitters and PLC RTD cards expect a Pt100 or Pt1000 curve and will read a thermistor wrongly.

You would also lose the IEC 60751 accuracy class and possibly the range above 150 degrees. For process duty keep the RTD and replace like for like with the same class and wiring.

What is the main disadvantage of a thermistor?

The main disadvantage is its strongly non linear curve, which needs a Beta or Steinhart Hart equation to convert resistance into temperature. Its useful range is also much narrower than that of a platinum sensor.

Thermistors are also more prone to self heating and to drift when kept near their upper limit. Low excitation current and a sensible temperature rating keep these problems under control.
